The Plain-brown woodcreeper Dendrocincla fuliginosa is a medium-sized furnariid that inhabits humid lowland forests from Honduras through Amazonia. Field studies indicate that newly hatched nestlings weigh approximately 6.35 grams [Ww0 = approximately 6.35 grams] at emergence from the egg, a modest initial mass consistent with the altricial developmental mode typical of most suboscine passerines. Growth proceeds rapidly under sustained parental provisioning, and by the end of the nestling period, females attain an ultimate wet weight of 36.55 grams [Wwi = 36.55 grams], whereas males reach a slightly larger asymptotic mass of 44.3 grams [Wwi = 44.3 grams]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with males averaging nearly twenty percent heavier than females, likely reflects sexual selection on male competitive ability during territory acquisition and mate defense. The incubation period itself is temperature-dependent; eggs maintained at a constant 31 °C hatch after approximately 23 days [ab = approximately 23 days] at 31 °C [T = 31 °C], a duration that falls within the typical range for furnariid birds rearing altricial young under warm, stable thermal conditions.

Respiratory metabolism trials conducted on active, post-absorptive adults under thermoneutral conditions reveal a substantial range in basal oxygen consumption. When measured at an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C, the maximum recorded resting metabolic rate reached 88.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 88.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a value that reflects the elevated energetic demands associated with the species' intense foraging activity and continuous bark-gleaning behavior on vertical trunks. This peak metabolic output is complemented by a somewhat lower, though still considerable, routine oxygen consumption rate of 67.27 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 67.27 milliliters of oxygen per hour] under the same thermal regime at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The relatively narrow range between peak and routine values suggests that these birds often operate close to their maximum aerobic capacity during normal daily activities, a pattern consistent with energetically costly substrate-gleaning foraging strategies observed in other woodcreepers.

The developmental schedule of Dendrocincla fuliginosa progresses through well-defined post-natal milestones when raised under ambient conditions typical of its lowland rainforest habitat. At the species' typical body temperature during activity, near 40.2 °C, the time from hatching to fledging is approximately 24 days [tx = approximately 24 days] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], after which the young bird departs the nest cavity and begins short, clumsy flights under continued parental supervision. Puberty, defined physiologically by the onset of gonadal maturation and gametogenesis, is attained comparatively quickly in this species; individuals reach sexual maturity at approximately 72 days following hatching [tp = approximately 72 days following hatching] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This abbreviated trajectory from a 6.35-gram hatchling to a reproductively capable adult in just over two months is remarkable for a bird of this body size and likely reflects strong selective pressure to secure breeding territories in a competitive, saturated forest understory environment.

Reproductive output in the Plain-brown woodcreeper follows a pattern of moderate fecundity paired with sustained breeding effort across a long adult life. Foraging adults operating at their active body temperature of 40.2 °C rarely produce more than two eggs per clutch, and the maximum annual laying rate corresponds to approximately two clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately two clutches per year] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], with each clutch comprising one to two eggs [N_R_i = each clutch comprising one to two eggs]. This limited per-event fecundity is counterbalanced by delayed but persistent reproductive effort; the age at which females first successfully produce a brood, measured from hatching, is 474.5 days [tR = 474.5 days] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The extended interval between fledging and first reproduction suggests that young birds require a lengthy period to acquire the foraging proficiency, molt into definitive adult plumage, and establish a suitable nest cavity or territory before initiating their own breeding attempts.

Longevity records for the Plain-brown woodcreeper indicate that individuals can persist for extraordinary periods relative to their body size. The maximum documented lifespan, measured from hatching under field conditions at the typical active body temperature of 40.2 °C, reaches 4161 days [am = 4161 days] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], which equates to more than eleven years. This exceptional longevity is among the highest recorded for any furnariid and is consistent with a life-history strategy emphasizing high adult survival and repeated, low-fecundity breeding attempts over many seasons. The combination of a single-egg or two-egg clutch, delayed first breeding near 474 days, protracted lifespan exceeding a decade, and moderate annual output of approximately two broods per year defines a slow-paced, bet-hedging demographic strategy. This long-lived, iteroparous life cycle is well-suited to the relatively stable, aseasonal conditions of Neotropical lowland forests, where competition for nest cavities and foraging substrates is intense and adult survivorship is the primary driver of population persistence.
